Package org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.bpmn.behavior

Class AdHocSubProcessActivityBehavior

java.lang.Object
org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.bpmn.behavior.FlowNodeActivityBehavior
org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.bpmn.behavior.AbstractBpmnActivityBehavior
org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.bpmn.behavior.AdHocSubProcessActivityBehavior
All Implemented Interfaces:
CoreActivityBehavior<ActivityExecution>, ActivityBehavior, CompositeActivityBehavior, ModificationObserverBehavior, SignallableActivityBehavior
public class AdHocSubProcessActivityBehavior extends AbstractBpmnActivityBehavior implements CompositeActivityBehavior, ModificationObserverBehavior
Runtime behavior of a BPMN adHocSubProcess.

No child is reached from the scope's own start. A child is started directly, by the activation API or by the entry list from CIB7-1891, and may reach others from there along the sequence flows between children that CIB7-1882 allows.

Notes on the parts that are not obvious from the code:

  • Entry starts only the entry list. execute(ActivityExecution) starts what activitiesToActivate names, if anything, and otherwise leaves the scope waiting.
  • initializeScope(org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.pvm.delegate.ActivityExecution, int) must honour numberOfInstances. Its caller, PvmAtomicOperationActivityInitStackNotifyListenerStart, passes 1 and immediately does get(0). That path is process-instance modification instantiating a dormant scope, not normal entry, so returning an empty list there would throw.
  • Both completion callbacks are reachable. tryPruneLastConcurrentChild is not involved: it runs only where the flow scope is the process definition, and an ad hoc child's flow scope is the ad hoc scope. What decides is PvmAtomicOperationActivityEnd. Every child runs on a concurrent execution, and one that is itself a scope hands its end to that concurrent execution as its own is removed, so every child ends through concurrentChildExecutionEnded(org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.pvm.delegate.ActivityExecution, org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.pvm.delegate.ActivityExecution). complete(org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.pvm.delegate.ActivityExecution) is reached by work running on the scope execution itself, which is an interrupting event sub process. Unlike parallel multi-instance, complete here is NOT "can't happen".

    • startEntryActivities

      protected void startEntryActivities(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      Starts the activities named by camunda:property activitiesToActivate, the declarative entry activation of CIB7-1891. Does nothing when the property is absent, which is every model written before it existed.

      Two behaviours here are deliberate and easy to get wrong.

      It runs after inactivate(), so the scope is in exactly the state the activation API finds it in. Anything else would make entry activation a second code path with its own bugs.

      And if the completion condition already holds, it starts nothing rather than refusing. The refusal that CIB7-1850 added throws, and throwing here would fail the process start outright — a model whose condition happens to be true on entry would become undeployable in practice. Starting nothing leaves the scope waiting, which is what CIB7-1851 decided such a scope does anyway.

    • resolveStartableChildren

      public List<ActivityImpl> resolveStartableChildren(ScopeImpl scope, Collection<String> activityIds, List<String> rejected)
      The children to start for the given ids, one per id and in the order given, so an id named twice is started twice. This is the one place both ways in -- the activation API and entry activation -- decide what a request means, which is why they cannot drift apart again (review finding 3 was the two copies disagreeing).

      An id that is not directly startable gets no child and is added to rejected instead, so that each caller refuses in its own terms: the API answers its caller, entry activation fails the start of the process.

    • findStartableChild

      public ActivityImpl findStartableChild(ScopeImpl scope, String activityId)
      The child to execute, which is not always the activity carrying the requested id.

      Loop characteristics make the parser wrap the activity: the direct child of the scope is a generated multi-instance body with the requested activity nested inside it. A recursive lookup would find the nested one, and executing that bypasses the body that owns the loop, so only direct children are considered and the generated body is resolved by name.

    • activityIdsOf

      public static List<String> activityIdsOf(Object value, String scopeId)
      The activity ids an entry list names. Shared by the parser, which checks a literal list at deployment, and by entry activation, which evaluates the expression when the scope is entered.

      A collection or an array gives its elements. Anything else is read as text. Text that starts with [ is a JSON array of ids -- which is what a Json variable holds, and an id, being an NCName, never starts with [. Any other text is a comma-separated list, which is what makes the static authoring form work: value="taskA,taskB" is a literal to the expression manager, so one path serves a literal list and an expression over process data alike.

    • doLeave

      public void doLeave(ActivityExecution execution)
      CIB7-1967. Hands the children's compensation subscriptions to the parent scope on the way out.

      The parser marks an ad hoc scope as consuming compensation, and a child may carry a compensation boundary event whose handler sits inside the scope. Those subscriptions live on the scope execution while it runs, and they die with it unless they are copied onto an event scope execution under the parent first. SubProcessActivityBehavior does exactly this, and an ad hoc scope has the same obligation for the same reason: without it, throwing compensation at the scope afterwards finds nothing and silently does nothing.

      The marker holding the scope's state is removed first. It is an event-scope child as well, and createEventScopeExecution moves every event-scope child into the compensation event scope, where the marker outlived the scope with its variables until the process ended (review finding 6). It belongs to the running scope, and the scope is leaving.

      Overrides:
      doLeave in class AbstractBpmnActivityBehavior

    • gatherResult

      protected void gatherResult(ActivityExecution scopeExecution, ActivityExecution endedExecution)
      Appends this performance's result to the gathering variable, if the scope gathers (CIB7-1892).

      Called as a child ends, and before the completion condition is consulted -- so a condition can be written against what has been gathered so far, which is the natural way to say "enough". One call site, not two: see complete(ActivityExecution) for why the other callback a child can end through is not one of them.

      Timing is the whole of it. The child's own output mapping has already run by now: an ad hoc child that carries one is a scope, and a scope executes its output parameters as it is destroyed, which happens before the flow scope's behaviour is notified. So the expression reads the value this performance produced, in the one moment it is still the current one -- the next performance of the same child overwrites it, and that is precisely the defect being answered.

      The list is rebuilt and written back rather than mutated in place, because a mutation of the value an entity already holds is not reliably detected as a change.

      Two rules make one expression serve every child of the scope: it is evaluated against the child that ended, so execution names that child, and a null result adds nothing. Between them a model can gather selectively -- ${execution.currentActivityId == 'tool' ? result : null} -- and record which performance produced an entry.

    • ensureFurtherActivationAllowed

      protected void ensureFurtherActivationAllowed(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      Refuses activation once the completion condition has held. Placed here rather than in ActivateAdHocSubProcessActivitiesCmd because process instance modification reaches the same two entry points without going through that command, and the rule is an invariant of the scope rather than of one API.

    • conditionHoldsNow

      protected boolean conditionHoldsNow(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      Evaluates the completion condition here and now, solely to decide whether to refuse activation.

      This is what makes FR-15 hold for a condition satisfied from outside the scope while every child is still running. The recorded flag cannot cover that case, because the condition is only ever evaluated when a child ends, so a condition nothing has observed leaves no trace. The two are complementary rather than redundant: the flag is a latch, so a condition that held once and has since gone false again still blocks activation, which is what "once the condition holds" means.

      It is deliberately not an evaluation point for completion. Nothing here completes the scope, so no deployed model changes outcome, and the entry semantics settled in CIB7-1851 are untouched. It costs one evaluation per activation request — an explicit, occasional operation — rather than the listener on every variable write that watching would need.

      An unresolvable condition means "cannot tell", and cannot-tell must not refuse. An unguarded ${x} throws before anything sets x, and refusing on that would move a modelling mistake's failure forward to the activation call for no benefit — the same trade that ruled out evaluating on entry, in miniature.

    • disposeOfRemainingChildren

      protected boolean disposeOfRemainingChildren(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      Disposes of whatever is still running once the completion condition has held, and says whether the scope may leave now.

      A child is still running when it is active or when its activity is null. The second case is a child that has entered a scope of its own -- an embedded sub process, or any activity carrying an io mapping -- where PvmAtomicOperationCreateScope inactivates the child and moves the live work one level down.

      CIB7-1961: the earlier form re-tested isActive() to decide whether to wait, after the outer condition had already been satisfied by the other disjunct. For a scope child neither branch then ran, the scope left with a live subtree beneath it, and deleting its execution violated ACT_FK_EXE_PARENT -- failing the very operation that satisfied the condition and leaving the instance unfinishable.

      Returns:
      true when nothing is left to wait for; false when cancelRemainingInstances is false and a child is still running, in which case the scope leaves when the last of them ends and this is reached again

    • cancelChild

      protected void cancelChild(ActivityExecution scopeExecution, ActivityExecution child, String reason)
      Cancels one child of a scope that is leaving, unless the child never started.

      A batch creates every child before it starts any, and createExecution() gives each the scope's own activity. If an earlier child ends the scope, the later ones are still standing on it, and cancelling them fires END on the scope itself -- which the scope fires again as it leaves (review finding 2). Nothing has run on such a child: its variables are set only when it starts, and it has no task and no activity instance of its own. So it is removed rather than cancelled.

    • completeScopeOnRequest

      public void completeScopeOnRequest(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      Ends the scope because a performer asked it to, rather than because a condition became true.

      BPMN 2.0.0 section 10.3.5 puts the performers in charge of when an ad hoc scope is finished, so there has to be a way to say so. Without it a scope whose completion condition never becomes true has no exit short of deleting the process instance.

      Cancels whatever is still running, regardless of cancelRemainingInstances. That attribute describes what happens when the completion condition is satisfied (Table 10.22); applying it here would let an explicit request to finish silently not finish, which is worse behaviour than either branch of the attribute was meant to produce.

      Unlike completeScope(org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.pvm.delegate.ActivityExecution, org.cibseven.bpm.engine.impl.pvm.delegate.ActivityExecution), this does not restore the scope's activity from an ended child, because there is no ended child: the scope execution is the target and already carries its own activity.

    • childTransitioned

      public void childTransitioned(ActivityExecution scopeExecution, ActivityExecution transitioning)
      A child has completed an activity and is taking a sequence flow to the next one (CIB7-1882).

      This is the fourth point at which the completion condition is consulted, and it exists because taking a flow is not an end: without it, a condition satisfied by the very completion that takes the flow would go unnoticed and the target would be performed regardless.

      What happens then is decided by cancelRemainingInstances, which is already the attribute that answers "what becomes of work in progress when the condition fires", rather than by a new rule. With the default true the target is not performed, which is what the latch from CIB7-1850 implies -- once the condition holds the scope starts nothing further. With false the scope waits for its survivors, and the target is performed, which is the guarantee BPMN 2.0.0 section 10.3.5 p.182 attaches to an inner flow.

      With true the path is also gathered here (CIB7-1892), because it never reaches the end where a path is otherwise gathered. What it has done is finished work, not remaining work: without this, a completed step was kept when no flow followed it and lost when one did. With false the path goes on and is gathered at its end, once.

      Without a completion condition there is nothing to consult: the no-condition rule is asked when a child ends, and taking a flow is not an end.

      protected void markActivated(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      Written once, on the first activation. Every later activation finds it set and writes nothing, so activating again costs no variable update and, with full history, no history row.

    • findStateExecution

      protected PvmExecutionImpl findStateExecution(ActivityExecution scopeExecution)
      CIB7-1850. The scope's state — the activation flag and the condition latch — lives on a dedicated event-scope child of the ad hoc scope rather than on the scope execution.

      The point is the variable resolution order. setVariable walks strictly up the parent chain and writes to the first ancestor that already holds the name; the scope execution is an ancestor of every ad hoc child, which is why a child could overwrite a variable kept there. A marker execution is a sibling of those children, so it is never on their walk-up path: a child writing this name creates its own variable at the process instance instead, and the engine's copy is untouched.

      Event scope is what keeps it out of the way of existing code — getNonEventScopeExecutions() is what child iteration, completion checks and delete cascade all use, so the marker is invisible to them without changing any of them.
